newsitem.title: USA: Panel says U.S. inflation overstated by 1.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: Panel says U.S. inflation overstated by 1.1 pct.

text.p: A congressionally appointed panel Wednesday estimated that government statistics overstate inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year, a finding with major implications for the U.S. budget and the whole economy.

Led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, the commission recommended the Clinton administration and Congress act to fix the problem, including possible legislation to alter the way tax brackets and costly programmes like Social Security are adjusted for cost-of-living changes.

"Congress and the president must decide whether they wish to continue widespread, substantial over-indexing of various federal spending programmes and features of the tax code," the five-member panel said. Quoting Congressional Budget Office estimates, its report said the upward bias in the Consumer Price Index would add $148 billion to the federal budget deficit by 2006 if not corrected.
Although the potential savings are huge, the political difficulties in agreeing to changes that could adversely affect voters were apparent at a news conference where the report was released.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said any CPI reform would require bipartisan effort, including leadership from President Bill Clinton.
"I want to stress that any action we take on this report must be broadly and deeply bipartisan," Roth said. "We must also have the full cooperation and leadership by the Clinton administration."
He urged quick action on the report and said he intended to hold hearings on the commission report early next year.
In a careful response, White House economic adviser Joseph Stiglitz said the administration would study the Boskin panel report as well as other views on measuring the cost of living.

"The Clinton administration believes that it is important to have the most accurate measure possible to ensure that Social Security and other benefits are protected from inflation and to adjust tax brackets to keep our tax system fair," Stiglitz said in a statement.

The report highlighted several reasons for the upward bias to the CPI including the difficulty in capturing the effects of changes in consumers' spending patterns and the impact of the introduction of new products.

It suggested that the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics take steps to improve technical problems with the CPI and that a new annual index be considered. It also suggested that a permanent independent group be set up to advise the BLS on various statistical and economic issues.
The commission recommended that Congress provide more money to improve the index and authorise information sharing between the Labour and Commerce Departments.

Boskin, an economic adviser to President George Bush who was named to head the panel last year by the Senate Finance Committee, said much of the CPI overstatement could be fixed but it would take a while. "We are all going to need some time," he told reporters.
